AI’s Original Sin is written into its training, says Parmy Olson

Anthropic PBC, when stripped of its no-hacking guardrails, resorted to lying to complete a cybersecurity challenge.

Parmy Olson

18 August, 2026 12:25 pm IST

Text Size: A- A+

Artificial intelligence models are trained not to lie to humans. Yet a funny thing is happening: AI has been lying to humans quite a bit.

Recently, an AI model made by Anthropic PBC that had been stripped of its no-hacking guardrails and given a cybersecurity challenge by the British government’s AI Security Institute, tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project hosted on the website GitHub. When it couldn’t solve the challenge using normal methods, it got creative. It researched the project’s human maintainers, created fake identities and then posed as software developers to gain the humans’ trust before trying to insert the bad code.

The AI Security Institute’s team noticed what was happening and shut the test down. Even with guardrails removed, the model shouldn’t have lied because Anthropic trained its model, Claude, to prioritize safety and honesty. Yet deception had “emerged as a by-product” as it tried to complete a difficult task, according to an incident report by the institute, which in a separate July study said that every new AI model it had tested for cheating had attempted it, and that such behavior would get harder to detect.

Be wary when leading AI companies say they can solve this problem. In playing God to create a greater form of intelligence, they’ve fallen prey to the same plotline as the Book of Genesis, and their creation has its own kind of original sin, called reinforcement learning.

Show Full Article

Reinforcement learning is one of the most effective methods of developing AI models and involves steering their behavior with praise and correction, much like training a dog. Instead of a hard-baked biscuit, the model gets a digital “treat” in the form of a numerical score, something like +1.5, or -2.0 for a bad answer.

When steered this way by thousands of independent contractors around the world (or, increasingly, by machine) models become polite and helpful. But the method can also lead to sycophancy and flattery, and it’s why AIs sometimes deceive. Driven to get a reward, they look for a shortcut, a phenomenon known as reward hacking. No matter how much Anthropic or OpenAI try to train their creations toward helpful behavior, their methods may be one of the biggest blockers to aligning AI with human values. “Reinforcement learning doesn’t reward truth or goodness,” says Connor Leahy, a former artificial-intelligence researcher who now runs the US arm of ControlAI, a non-profit trying to stop the development of superintelligent AI systems. “It rewards passing the test by any means necessary.”

That could mean tricking someone or inadvertently causing some kind of harm. One example in the wild points to where that could go. Earlier this year, a technologist in Australia named Andrew Bird asked Anthropic’s Claude to help him get into a popular gym class. The AI agent, built on the open-source OpenClaw framework  and able to carry out tasks on the Internet ended up exploiting a vulnerability in the gym’s online systems to book him weeks in advance.

When he asked to go up a class’s waiting list, Claude cancelled the reservation of the person sitting at the top, and moved Bird from fourth place to third, according to an interview Bird gave this month. (This appears to have been personal project of Bird’s, who wrote about the experience in a now-deleted blog post for Affinda Holdings Pty Ltd, where he is head of AI. Affinda didn’t respond to requests for comment.)

Such incidents are rare because the use of AI agents is still largely limited to software developers and tech enthusiasts. But OpenAI, Anthropic and their larger competitors are pushing the general public to ask chatbots to carry out tasks for them online. Mark Zuckerberg said last month that Meta Platforms Inc. was developing personal agents as a “great consumer product that just works out of the box and is easy enough for billions of people.”

Zuckerberg hasn’t said if his AI assistants will book you onto a gym class, but we may be looking at a future where many more people ask AI to help them get a refund or book the best seats at a show and their agents simply treat other humans as obstacles to those tasks. That might mean cancelling other reservations, interfering with rival bidders in an online auction or, in the case of seeking compensation, fabricating evidence.

Efforts by AI companies so far don’t look promising. In January, Anthropic, which has long positioned itself as the most safety conscious AI developer, published a revised, 23,000-word constitution for Claude to shape its behavior for the good. Yet when the AI Security Institute ran its latest tests, most of the “unsanctioned” actions it recorded came from the Mythos 5 model produced by Anthropic.In the real world, a long document about honesty and privacy can’t account for the near-infinite potential scenarios that Claude may find itself in.

Simply telling a model not to cheat doesn’t seem to help much. When the research nonprofit METR told a model released by OpenAI in 2025 not to cheat, it did so just as often as before. It also broke the rules in 14 of 20 attempts at a task when told its work would help scientists researching Alzheimer’s disease.

“This is not the kind of problem that some engineers can solve with math,” says Leahy. “This is a problem that a whole civilization, all of our greatest mathematicians, philosophers, scientists [need to] work on for generations to make incremental progress.”

There’s no question that Anthropic puts considerable effort into AI’s moral steering, and people close to Dario Amodei tell me the company’s CEO is genuine in his desire to build the technology safely. But even he cannot escape a powerful commercial imperative that drives people — and increasingly AI — to win at all costs. That is how Silicon Valley itself created such unfathomable wealth while causing reverberant harms in human life. When technologists build a system optimized for winning, don’t be surprised when it does exactly that.

Appeasement has a bad name in India. Time is ripe to use it in foreign policy

A strategic culture that puts a premium on assertion and displays of strength may have been more counterproductive than beneficial to Indian interests in some cases.

Sidharth Raimedhi

T here is no room in Indian strategic culture for a policy of ‘appeasement’, which is unfortunate in the present context. The popular narrative of appeasement as a form of craven diplomacy resorted to by the weak in order to pacify the strong is an unfortunate distortion of reality as well as the concept. The popular imagination of Chamberlain’s short-sighted policy of feeding Hitler’s appetite through concession-making and Nehru’s opening of the door to the post-colonial world for the PRC at the Bandung Conference are still the sum total of what our strategic culture thinks of as ‘appeasement’.

But historical record shows that it has often been used by major and great powers to realign interests with potential adversaries in order to pursue core power and security interests more efficiently. Britain’s appeasement of the US in the 1900s and Stalin’s appeasement of imperial Japan in the 1930s are strong examples in this regard.

There is a reason why the time is ripe for India to examine the methods and rewards of a policy of appeasement. India is contending with systemic economic strain and its military capabilities are mired in structural challenges – from procurement delays to indigenisation and modernisation. It can be argued that India’s relative military power is decreasing vis-à-vis the loose constellation of adversaries that now stands arrayed against it. In the 2010s, Indian military officials  spoke confidently  of India being able to handle a two-front war against Pakistan and China. The zeitgeist has shifted since, and the list of adversaries has also grown. At the same time, India’s much-anticipated manufacturing take-off  failed to occur in the last decade — requiring a macro-policy reboot if India is to attain political stability at home and military preparedness to face the challenges of future warfare.

Show Full Article

India now faces a more hostile Pakistan that is being equipped by both Turkey and China’s future-ready defence-industrial base, which enables scale through affordability, speed due to quick procurement-deployment cycles and lethality through the setting up of complex networked kill-chains. To its west, India is also witnessing a growing list of quasi-adversaries such as Azerbaijan and Turkey. The recent Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signals that India may have to brace for a possible downturn in ties with Saudi Arabia. Most crucially, the future of India-Bangladesh ties remains greatly uncertain. The countries’ still-souring relations are set to deepen both Chinese and Pakistani influence in Dhaka, as both Delhi and Dhaka seek to exercise leverages in the absence of any new shared understanding of future progress and stabilisation.

Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, accompanied by their ministers of Foreign Affairs and Defence, pose after signing a joint defence agreement in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, August 7, 2026. | REUTERS A strategic culture that puts a premium on assertion and displays of strength has moved India toward leverage-cards in managing ties with Bangladesh as well as Turkey and Azerbaijan. India’s military support to Armenia, recent spurt of engagement with Cyprus and tolerance of Sheikh Hasina’s speeches from Delhi are all examples of this. However, a careful examination of the record also suggests that such an approach may have been more counterproductive than beneficial to Indian interests. This may be because the leverages themselves are not strong enough to effect the desired changes in the other’s strategic orientation.

Given that we now face strong domestic economic challenges, a growing list of quasi-adversaries and under-delivering leverage-cards, there is cause for broadening our strategic lens and adding more arrows in the quiver.

Appeasement has a bad name Appeasement has acquired an unenviable reputation since 1939. It is crucial to understand the origins as well as sustainment of this ever since.

The reputation problem lies in the simple fact that the western strategic elite consensus, popularised through mass media and textbooks, sought a simple story that explained the road to the Second World War. It was useful to blame one person, Neville Chamberlain, and his policy of appeasement for emboldening Hitler. On the other side of the Atlantic, President Roosevelt himself was hopeful that the agreement reached at Munich had successfully satisfied Hitler’s grievances and prevented an outbreak of war. This formed the association between weak-willed pragmatic concessions and encouragement of further grievance, territorial greed and expansion. Interestingly, the Anglo-American strategic consensus found great resonance even in a newly post-colonial India.

Churchill’s own heroic  account of the war  — accepted by mainstream historians — necessitated a negative contrast to his own projected image of a maverick and defiant war leader who possessed gumption, moral clarity and courage. More conveniently forgotten is the record of Churchill himself  appeasing Stalin’s appetite for territory , justifiably perhaps, in Eastern Europe from at least 1943 and in line with realpolitik. Roosevelt was no less keen in this initiative.

Winston Churchill, Franklin D. Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin at the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the Allies negotiated the post-war order in Europe | Commons As the Second World War ended, the US swung to the other extreme of power projection and  pursued a strategy of absolute security and forward basing that required a moral resolve against negotiating ‘spheres of influence’ with the Soviet Union. In other words, a Pax Americana based on a preponderance of power left little room for appeasement as a form of realpolitik. It was only after the setback in Vietnam that the US began appreciating the limits to its power, thereby opening the door toward appeasement of communist China.

With a return to triumphalism after winning the Cold War, the US’ wars in the Middle East themselves relied significantly on the ‘Munich’ analogy in order to override and silence sceptics and peace activists. This applies as much to Saddam’s Iraq and Gaddafi’s Libya as it does to Trump and Netanyahu’s war on Iran.

Appeasement and power-maximisation But there are scores of examples, other than Chamberlain and Hitler, where appeasement has not led to disaster but to success. While the word appeasement has been popularised by its most stark failure, its stories of success are unsung. This is a point that the historian of great powers Paul Kennedy very aptly noted in his  1976 essay  “The tradition of appeasement in British foreign policy”. It is another matter that critics of Chamberlain ignore how closely tied his policy of appeasement was to British rearmament itself— but that is a subject for another day.

Britain’s deliberate policy of appeasement toward the US throughout the 1890s yielded the great success that is now known as ‘ the Great Rapprochement’ . This policy entailed the sacrifice of British interests in the Western hemisphere, but achieved in return the fulfilment of its core interest: the prevention of German hegemony in Europe in alliance with the US. Britain’s own imperial expansion and consolidation in the Indian subcontinent after 1857 relied heavily on appeasing various power centres from time to time. This included the princely states through the Royal Proclamation of 1858, and various sub-groups ranging from Afghans and Sikhs to Gurkhas.

An 1898 poster celebrating growing ties between Britain and the US during the Great Rapprochement | Commons The US’ own appeasement of communist China from the early 1970s (such as making concessions on the One China principle and supporting the PRC’s representation at the UN) achieved the required strategic reorientation to arrange overwhelming forces against the Soviet Union to win the Cold War.

No less a practitioner of cold realpolitik than Josef Stalin himself embarked on a policy of appeasement toward Imperial Japan after the latter’s takeover of Manchuria in 1931.

Facing industrial setbacks, a still-nascent defence industry and adversaries on both fronts, Stalin offered and delivered one significant concession after another to Imperial Japan after its entry into Manchuria. These included non-aggression pacts, favourable commercial agreements, acceptance of the puppet state of Manchukuo, the selling of stakes in the Manchurian railway, the closing down of Chinese consulates in the Far East and restraint in response to provocative Japanese attacks on Soviet patrol boats. Stalin did so in order to avert a possible  pre-emptive Japanese attack on the Russian Far East  before Soviet military power was prepared. He sought to buy time until the five-year plans enabled a stronger deployment of forces in the Far East by the end of the decade.

By decisively crushing Japanese forces in 1939 — after relying on years of appeasement — Stalin ensured that his rear flank was secure for the entire span of the coming war with Nazi Germany. Appeasement is almost always borne of constraints, but its aim is always to maximise power and achieve security interests.

China itself undertook a form of appeasement toward post-Soviet Russia from the late 1990s with the aim of ensuring that Russia never chose to pursue a policy of balancing China’s rise in Eurasia — from Central Asia to the Korean peninsula. Beijing, after all, wisely sought to break the cycle of revenge between the two Eurasian great powers in order to secure its own rise.

Appeasement and its conditions and caveats I offer these brief examples just to underscore the observation that appeasement is not just a defensible policy but also the most efficient recourse at times, depending on circumstances. This does not mean that it is always guaranteed to succeed. There are notable failures (beyond Munich) as well. The literature on the subject also offers useful caveats. For instance, it is wiser to appease the weak than to appease the strong. One can think here of the potential folly of seeking to appease China.

Furthermore, if pursued when one is too weak, the appeased state may indeed interpret concessions as a sign of weakness — inviting further trouble and provocations. But this simply clarifies that it is a form of strategic policy like any other — such as coercion, alliance-making, deterrence, spheres of influence, war, and mediation. Its application and success depend on circumstances, investments, the nature of the adversary, a sense of timing and so on.

A dramatic failure of one singular policy of deterrence, after all, does not sully the entire concept of deterrence as a form of strategic policy. No less a critic of appeasement than Churchill himself clarified the matter in an  address  to Parliament in 1950: “Appeasement from weakness and fear is alike futile and fatal. Appeasement from strength is magnanimous and noble and might be the surest and perhaps the only path to world peace.”

When a polity or a strategic culture erases the concept and policy of appeasement as a legitimate option, it inevitably shrinks its own range of options vis-à-vis its strategic challenges.

Indian strategic culture’s wariness of appeasement There are a myriad of sociological, political and strategic reasons why ‘appeasement’ as a deliberate medium- to long-term strategic policy never held much appeal in the Indian strategic mindscape. In the present context, it evokes an almost negative response given the prevalent perception of India marching toward great power status and finally asserting its weight on the regional and world stage. In such a zeitgeist, appeasement — even when national interest demands it — risks causing cognitive dissonance and negative self-perception.

Historically, a loose association with Colonial Britain’s policy of ‘appeasement’ toward minorities had sullied the concept and idea since the early 20th century. Its extension into the realm of domestic politics (the right-wing charge against secular appeasement) had only reinforced this negative association.

In terms of foreign policy, a certain reading of the road to the 1962 India-China war as resulting from Nehru’s ‘appeasement’ policy towards China was a striking — yet distorted — retelling of the Chamberlain-Hitler morality play. More contemporary historical accounts —  as noted earlier  — now ironically place as much blame for the war on Nehru’s intransigence towards China on the boundary issue as on his supposed idealism or naivete.

Also Read: Three countries, no common enemy—why the Mecca defence pact is weaker than it looks

Can appeasement work for India? Post-colonial Indian strategic culture’s insecure fixation with displays of strength and weakness leads to very little political (and intellectual) capital in the hands of a government that might seek to pursue a longer-term policy of appeasement toward potential adversaries. Hence, even as there is a desire to improve relations with Turkey and Bangladesh, efforts toward the same have generally become mired in mutual recriminations as well as alternating tactical measures between conciliation and strong-arming.

Every indication of a more positive momentum borne of pragmatism is soon followed by a more dramatic setback caused by fresh grievance. As India’s strategic landscape becomes increasingly and unprecedentedly challenging, ideas such as relying on improved relations with Cyprus to signal leverage to Turkey and leveraging remnants of the Awami League to extract better behaviour from Dhaka are likely to be counterproductive.

India shares an enclosed region with two nuclear-armed powers that each claim an Indian state for itself. The China-Pakistan strategic partnership has gone from strength to strength, while the India-US strategic partnership is being reconsidered. In this landscape, India is obliged to ensure that its growing list of additional potential adversaries — from Turkey to Bangladesh to Saudi Arabia — is reduced. Relying on brief sprouts of engagement followed by coercive signalling may not deliver the same. This is why India needs to give more thought and consideration to the objective of affecting strategic orientations through policies of appeasement while building economic and military power in the background.
